title: Haunted house? Ghost stories bring history to life at Gorgas House Museum
excerpt: From ghost stories to experiential learning, the Gorgas House Museum uses nearly 200 years of history to engage students and visitors.
content:
From its transition from a dining hall, infirmary, post office and lecture rooms, the Gorgas House Museum’s most memorable role of its nearly 200-year history continues to be its time as a home to the Gorgas family. Any historic building with such a storied past tends to become home to ghost stories and paranormal legend, and the Gorgas House Museum is no different.

“We have different categories of the ghost stories we like telling. Some are clearly explainable. And then we have the category of ‘I don’t know what that’s about,’ and we’re just going to keep it that way,” explained Sonya Harwoord-Johnson, director of the Gorgas House Museum. 

Whether or not spirits actually dwell within the building’s halls, the museum has embraced these legends as a way to engage students and visitors in the fascinating history of campus and the state.

Home of the “Campus Mother”

Throughout the house’s 197 years on campus, its most famous resident is Tuscaloosa native Amelia Gayle Gorgas. After moving to Washington, D.C., to organize political events and fundraisers during her father’s term as Alabama’s governor, she returned to Tuscaloosa when her husband, Josiah, became UA’s President. 

Less than a year into Josiah’s term as University President, a series of strokes forced his resignation. As a retirement gift, the Alabama Board of Trustees gifted Josiah the honorary title of University librarian as well as the Gorgas House (formerly called the Pratt House), for his family to reside in.

Josiah passed in the house shortly after, leaving Amelia to assume the role of University librarian. Drawing on her experience as First Lady, Amelia organized statewide donations to increase library collections by over 20,000 volumes. In 1925, the campus’ main library was named in her honor, marking the first academic building on campus to be named after a woman. 

During her time as University librarian, Amelia was also appointed postmistress and matron of the university infirmary, roles that operated out of her home.

Because students relied on her for library books, mail and medical care, Amelia quickly earned the title of “campus mother,” according to Harwood-Johnson.

“I always say that this house kind of operated as the student center before the student center was built. Anytime you needed anything, you went to Mrs. Gorgas. She knew how things were run. If you were homesick, she would help you get a letter back home or get letters from home to come back in,” she explained. 

Because she was so beloved by students, the yearbook was dedicated to her for six consecutive years, and the class of 1886 also gifted her handwritten poems and a one-of-a-kind trophy. These tributes remain on display at the Gorgas House Museum. 

Turning the unexplained into education

Over the years, some museum staff and visitors have claimed they hear echoes of the house’s history in the form of unexplained sights and sounds. 

When working alone in the house, staff have reported seeing Amelia in her green obituary gown, as well as hearing footsteps going up and down the stairs followed by the swish of a dress. The eyes of her portrait, as well as her sister’s, have been said to follow guests throughout the home. 

Interns describe Amelia’s music box, which can be viewed on tours, playing without being winded, or hearing coughing from the upstairs bedroom where the infirmary used to reside. 

With six residents having died in the Gorgas House, the rumor of supernatural occurrences drew the attention of paranormal investigators, who examined the home in 2025.

The Gorgas House Museum’s unexplained phenomena have inspired interns to create the Halloween exhibit, “Calling the Spirits In: Spiritualism in America.” The display showcases the spiritual movement that occurred after the Civil War, with civilians attempting to contact loved ones who died in battle. New technology emerged from this period, such as postmortem photography, which was used to process grief from unexpected causalities. 

Playing into the spooky season, the Alabama Museum of Natural History and Gorgas House Museum have partnered to create “Haunting at the Museums.” This year’s Haunting at the Museums is “Otherworldly Encounters,” an event that combines the phenomena of spirits with science and space research.

The museum’s exploration of the supernatural also extends beyond curated exhibits. Giving life to the stories that have been brewing for decades, the Museum began offering annual Haunted Tours.

“I think Halloween is one of our coolest [museum events] because one of my main goals of this house is to break down preconceived notions or barriers about what museums are,” Harwood-Johnson said. “When we tell the ghost stories, everyone’s super excited. We can sprinkle a little bit of history or a little bit more information so that it can be spooky and educational, or it can be engaging and educational and fun. Then you learn without realizing you’re learning.”

More than a museum

In addition to creating seasonal programming, Harwood-Johnson’s team of over 20 student interns uses the museum as a hub for experiential learning. Her interns include aerospace engineering students who tabulate data and contribute to the Gorgas House blog, marketing students who create social media content, elementary education students who plan lessons for field trips, history majors who conduct focused research and others who give tours and curate exhibits.

Beyond student involvement, the museum has also partnered with researchers on campus and across the world. One UA construction engineering professor is currently experimenting with new technologies to scan the Gorgas House Museum and create a 3D digital model of it. Last year, the Haunting at the Museum was presented in partnership with a museum in Bangkok, where each museum contained one half of the exhibit.   

Throughout academic partnerships across a plethora of fields, Harwood-Johnson hopes for the Gorgas House Museum to operate as an interdisciplinary hub of nontraditional education. 

“It has so many different roles of working as this lab of experiential learning of providing a space where students can get hands-on experience in a wide variety of careers.”

Visitors wanting to learn more about the Gorgas House Museum and its programming can visit Calling the Spirits In: Spiritualism in America until Oct. 28, 2026, while Otherworldly Encounters occurs on Oct. 27, 2026, from 5-8 p.m. for lovers of mystery, history and science.
